description: Ludilume Studios built Earth Trend Detective: pick any place on Earth and a question, and 45 years of NASA data give an honest answer on whether it is really changing. Team: Talha Abid (Pakistan) and Kainat Ijaz (USA).
summary: Earth Trend Detective is a free website that lets anyone check whether the Earth is really changing where they live. Search for a place or click the map, then ask a question such as "Is it getting hotter?". The tool gets up to 45 years of monthly NASA data for that place (NASA POWER, built on the MERRA-2 model and CERES satellites), removes the seasons, and runs two statistical tests that must agree. It answers in plain words: yes, maybe, not significant yet (with an estimate of how many more years of data would settle it), or no detectable trend. A map then tests every grid cell around the place to show where the same variable is rising, falling or not changing. For average temperature it also gives a second opinion from the nearest of 6,717 weather station records, and says plainly when the thermometer and the NASA model disagree. Four step-by-step examples, including greenness from the MODIS satellite, show students how to be data detectives. It matters because "it's getting hotter" is easy to say and hard to check: one hot year is not a trend, and an honest "we can't tell yet" is still a useful answer.
details:
Try it in 30 seconds

Open https://earth-trend-detective.vercel.app and click "Are Jacobabad's nights warming?". You get a verdict, three key numbers, a band of year stripes and the charts. Then press "Map where it is changing nearby". Demo video (29 seconds): https://earth-trend-detective.vercel.app/demo. Source code (MIT licence): https://github.com/talhaabidj/earth-trend-detective

What makes it different

  • It can answer "not yet": when a trend is not significant, it estimates how many more years of data would settle it.
  • It only says "yes" when two different tests agree, and one of them allows for month-to-month memory in the data.
  • Its map tests hundreds of grid cells at once and filters out chance results, so "where is it changing?" gets an honest answer.
  • It gives no verdict on data that cannot support one: places with no data, values that never change, or values that are zero in most months.
  • Every result links to its exact NASA data request, and the statistics are checked by 23 automatic tests, so anyone can verify it.

What it does

Earth Trend Detective follows the four steps the challenge asks for.

  1. Choose variables. 14 NASA variables in four themes (heat; rain and water; air and sky; snow and cold), each with a one-line definition and a reason it matters. One-click starter questions get a first-time visitor to a result at once, and a helper suggests where to start for a city, desert, mountains, farmland, rainforest or coast.
  2. Get the data for a region. Search a city, click the map or use your own location, anywhere on Earth. Use one grid cell (about 50 km) or a 2° × 2° area, averaged by cell size. The data comes straight from the NASA POWER service in the visitor's browser.
  3. See the time series. Monthly values from 1981 to 2025 (2001 to 2025 for sunlight and cloud), in tabs: the series with seasons removed, with yearly averages and the trend line with its 95% range; the raw series; the usual seasonal cycle; and a yearly table. Each result also shows three key numbers and a band of year stripes (blue for years below usual, red for years above), so the change can be seen at a glance. A second place can be put next to the first to compare.
  4. Test it. Two tests must agree before the tool says "yes": the seasonal Mann-Kendall test, with the Sen slope as the rate and its 95% range; and a straight-line fit whose significance test allows for month-to-month memory in the data, which makes simple tests over-confident. If the trend is not significant, the tool estimates how many more years of data would give a 90% chance of detecting it (Weatherhead et al. 1998), because, as the challenge says, sometimes all a trend needs is a longer record.

Where is it changing?

The map tests every grid cell in a 6° or 10° box (up to about 340 cells). Because so many tests are run at once, about 1 in 20 would look significant by chance, so a cell only counts as a clear trend if it also passes a Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery check. For example, daytime high temperatures around Lahore show a band of clear falls along the Punjab plains (72 of 320 cells), no clear rises, and no clear trend in most of the surrounding area.

What the examples found

  • Jacobabad, Pakistan, one of the hottest cities on Earth: the average temperature shows no detectable trend since 1981, but night-time lows rise by 0.35 °C per decade (95% range 0.23 to 0.48). Daytime highs show no trend. The answer depends on what you measure.
  • Lahore and Phoenix (USA): humidity rises by 2.9% per decade in Lahore and falls by 1.7% in Phoenix; daytime highs fall in Lahore (−0.27 °C per decade) and rise in Phoenix (+0.36 °C). The same variable moves in opposite directions in two places.
  • Hunza, in the Karakoram: daytime highs are not significant yet (+0.10 °C per decade, range −0.03 to +0.23); about 30 more years of data would settle it. The average temperature is clearly rising (+0.21 °C per decade).
  • Greener from space: MODIS greenness (NDVI) rises in central Lahore and in a spot in the Thar desert since 2000; for Thar, MERRA-2 soil wetness, a separate NASA dataset, rises too.

We do not claim causes for these trends. The tool finds change; explaining it is the next step. A check against weather stations (see the next section) found that the stations at Jacobabad and Lahore show the average temperature rising, which the NASA model does not.

Why the numbers can be trusted

Our Mann-Kendall code matches the pymannkendall library, and our Sen slope and its 95% range match SciPy. The browser and Python versions of the statistics give the same numbers, and the tests run automatically on every change. Each example states the verdict it expects, and the build stops if the data disagrees, so no story text can contradict the numbers. Known traps are handled: POWER's extra "annual" month and missing-value codes are removed, gaps are never filled, and the sunlight and cloud variables start in 2001 so that a change of satellite product cannot look like a trend. Odd data gets a plain message, not a misleading verdict: places with no data, values that never change (soil wetness over open ocean), and values that are zero in most months (snow in a desert). Limits are stated on the site: POWER is a model-based product at about 50 km, not a weather station, and a straight-line trend is a summary. We also checked POWER's average temperature against weather station records (NOAA GHCN-Monthly v4, the station data behind NASA's GISTEMP) at five places. At Phoenix, Manaus and Svalbard the station and POWER both show clear warming. At Jacobabad and Lahore the stations show clear warming (+0.26 and +0.29 °C per decade) that POWER does not. So for those two cities our examples report what the NASA model shows, and the city thermometers disagree. We report this as it is: the site's limits and both examples now say so, and the full table is in METHODS.md, section 7.

Who it is for and what we hope to achieve

Students, teachers and curious people can answer their own questions about their own places with NASA data, without a login, code or statistics training, and learn that "not significant yet" is a real scientific answer. The site includes a 15-minute classroom activity, works on phones, has light and dark themes, can be used with a keyboard, and has no issues in an automated accessibility check (WCAG 2.1 AA). We started with places in Pakistan, where heat and water stress are part of daily life, and the tool works anywhere on Earth.

How it is creative, and what we considered

Most trend tools draw a line and stop. Ours gives a verdict that can be "not yet", says how long to wait, and only says "yes" when two different tests agree. The year stripes and the three key numbers make each result readable in seconds, and the map shows where a trend holds and where it flips. We chose honesty over drama: no claims about causes, limits shown beside every result, and chance results filtered out. We also planned for real use: the examples work even when NASA's servers are busy, the site needs no sign-up and has no ads or tracking, and it runs on a phone on a slow connection. It also checks itself: for average temperature, each result shows a second opinion from the nearest long weather station record (6,717 stations worldwide, same tests) and states plainly when the thermometer does not agree with the NASA model.

Tools

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no build step) for the website, with our own SVG charts, Leaflet maps with OpenStreetMap tiles and Open-Meteo's free geocoding for the place search. Python with NumPy and SciPy for the statistics engine, examples and tests; pytest and Node for the tests; GitHub and GitHub Actions; Vercel (free plan) for hosting; Playwright and FFmpeg to make the demo video from screenshots of the site, with a voice-over recorded by a team member.

References

Hirsch, Slack & Smith (1982), seasonal Mann-Kendall test; Sen (1968) and Gilbert (1987), slope and its range; Santer et al. (2000), autocorrelation and effective sample size; Weatherhead et al. (1998), years needed to detect a trend; Benjamini & Hochberg (1995) and Benjamini & Yekutieli (2001), false discovery rate; Hussain & Mahmud (2019), pymannkendall. The year stripes are inspired by Ed Hawkins's "warming stripes" (showyourstripes.info, CC BY 4.0) and are drawn by our own code from NASA data. Challenge resources we read: Giovanni (NASA GES DISC), the NASA NTRS paper on SeaWiFS chlorophyll time series, and the KNMI Climate Explorer.

The data was obtained from National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Langley Research Center's Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources (POWER) project funded through the NASA Earth Science Division (POWER Monthly and Annual API v2.10.0, accessed 14–15 November 2026). Not an official NASA product.
